title: Enlightenment
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett's talk explores two approaches to Buddhist practice: systematic methods that aim for a specific goal of awakening, and trust methods that focus on cultivating a sense of freedom and wholeness through non-attachment and openness. Nomon suggests that these two approaches can be complementary, with the systematic method offering insight into our brokenness and the trust method offering a path to healing and transformation. By embracing both perspectives, practitioners can deepen their understanding of themselves and cultivate greater compassion, trust, and freedom in their practice.

So, Chris Seth and with my agreement, I did sign off on this, we thought of this topic for these Sunday talks: enlightenment.
When somebody says on the phone, "Hey, let's talk about enlightenment," it's easy to say, "Yeah, that sounds nice.
We should definitely talk about enlightenment."
And then you sit down to write a talk about enlightenment.
You're like, oh, no.
And if I remember right, maybe this was just a dream I had, Chris's first talk in January, she also listed off a whole bunch of people who she said were not enlightened, including me.
So now I really feel in a pickle.
It's so interesting that we have this tradition.

If you read the textbook descriptions of Buddhism or go to the encyclopedia, it says that Buddhism has this goal of enlightenment or awakening, nirvana, complete freedom from conditioning and suffering.
Sometimes that kind of entry will have a little more nuance and say, well, enlightenment is the specialty of the monks and nuns.

The lay people support them, but they receive a sort of secondary positive effect from their support of the monastics through this mysterious thing called merit, a kind of beneficial energy from good actions.
And what's the best good action in that system?
Not surprisingly, one of the best good actions is supporting the monastics.
So it's all pretty mysterious, actually, even though most of us come to Zen in a much more practical, non-mystical framework, I think.
We want a little peace, right?
We want a little ease.
We don't want to be so tangled up.
We don't want to suffer so much.
Then I couldn't help thinking a little bit about the words involved, since I was writing, in the realm of words.
Enlightenment is an English word, of course, and these traditions were not created in English.
In the European tradition, the age of enlightenment followed the shifts of culture from the Renaissance and the beginnings of the scientific revolution.
The age of enlightenment is, quote, this is from Wikipedia:
*An intellectual and philosophical movement that dominated the world of ideas in Europe in the 17th and 18th centuries.

The Enlightenment, capital E, included a range of ideas centered on the sovereignty of reason and the evidence of the senses as the primary sources of knowledge, and advanced ideas such as liberty, progress, toleration, fraternity, constitutional government, separation of church and state.*
So the growth of reason is the Western Enlightenment, paying more attention to evidence, not just taking things on from the priest, presumably.

We pretty much take that for granted, except it's upsetting and shocking when it seems like other people in our societies aren't doing that, aren't acting in a way that seems rational and based on the evidence.
Certainly the Age of Enlightenment is also a work in progress.
Trumpism seems to have shown that.
But this word Enlightenment, in the Western tradition, has a certain rational, intellectual, evidence-based, deep root.
The article goes on to say that some date the beginning of the Enlightenment, capital E, to maybe 1630.
Cogito ergo sum: I think, therefore, I am.
And yet Buddhism seems to have a really different orientation around being.
We make jokes about "I think, therefore, I am" in Zen halls, right?
That "I am" doesn't exactly have to do with thinking, that thinking is an obscuration of what I truly am.
So maybe we say, "I let go of thinking, therefore, I am," or "I experience my deeper am-ness," or something.
There's some conflict here.
We talk about Enlightenment: what Enlightenment are we talking about?
Rationality?
Beyond rationality?
Both?
Either?
But anyway, maybe Enlightenment is the wrong word.
Some prefer awakening.
Awakening is maybe a better translation of one of the main Sanskrit terms, B-O-D-H-I, bodhi.
The word buddha has the same root as bodhi.
And we think of bodhisattvas and bodhicitta and bodhi this and bodhi that, so maybe awakening is better.
The nice thing about awakening is that there's a process of awakening.
Enlightenment sounds like a thing that's done.
Awakening is maybe never quite done.
We just keep exploring, we keep living into awakening as a verb.

But it would be negligent of me, or maybe avoidant of me, not to acknowledge that the tradition also has a strong thread that does say, even amidst this field of teachings about impermanence and process, the endless flow of causality, that this awakening is a permanent and radical sea change in the way that a being is.
A freedom, ongoing freedom from suffering, conditioning.
So that's in there too.
And that's what so impressed the Western scene in the 1950s and 60s and so on, like, whoa, far out, that kind of change.
I was reading a koan commentary by Robert Aitken, we talk about him a lot.
In this koan he was admiring what the psychologist Eric Fromm, innovative humanistic psychologist, wrote in 1960.
He was studying with D.T.
Suzuki.
He wrote:
*The full awakening to reality means, in psychological terms, to obtain a fully "productive orientation."
This means not to relate to the world only receptively, exploitively, accordingly, or in the market fashion, but creatively, actively.
In the state of full productiveness, there are no veils which separate me from not me.
The object is not an object anymore.
It doesn't stand against me, but is with me.*
That's interesting, the use of the word productive, not the way I usually think about productive.
We're not hoarding, we're not exploiting, we're not transactional, like a marketplace, getting what we want, trying to avoid this and that.
But we're creative, we're active, and nothing is separating us from what we thought of before, mistakenly, as not us, not me.
Integrated, right?
Integrated.
I was appreciating another source here, Gil Franzdal.
Somebody mentioned to me she was doing a distance course with Gil Franzdal on breathing, great idea.
Gil was early on a Zen practitioner in our school at San Francisco Zen Center.
I met him there when I started, and then later he went on to be a Vipassana teacher and a scholar, an interesting contemporary source.
Lives down here somewhere.
Anyway, Gil did a translation of the classic text, the Dhammapada.
I've read a million quotations from the Dhammapada, early Buddhist poem, but never really studied it, so I got ahold of Gil's translation.
In his introduction he talks about this question of what's the goal of practice, in a useful way.
I've edited this down a little bit.
Gil says:
*The Dhammapada, like the early Buddhist tradition, offers two distinct goals for what in Western terms could be called the spiritual life.
The verses in this text can frequently, and even suddenly, switch to emphasize one or the other goal.
The first goal focuses on attaining happiness and welfare, in this life or in future lives.
To attain this goal, the verses emphasize virtuous action and ethical teachings.
They're teachings on living by ethical precepts, watching and disciplining one's mind, being without hate, being respectful, avoiding evil deeds, being nonviolent, curbing anger.
Many of these are not uniquely Buddhist teachings.
Some may have been adapted from poetry, songs, and teachings already current in India when Buddha came along.*
So two goals.
The first goal is happiness.
That's why we're here, but our minds here, there's a second goal?
Wait.
We won't do it all.
The first goal explains the second goal.
Gil continues:
*The second, ultimately and uniquely Buddhist goal, described in these early teachings, is liberation.

This is a form of spiritual freedom that involves a radical personal change, consists of purification, often described forcefully as the elimination or destruction of one's mental defilements, of one's attachments, of one's hindrances.
Since these mental forces keep a person bound up in the cycle of rebirth, when they're overcome, a practitioner is liberated from these cycles.*
Forcefully.
So in early Buddhism there's this tie-in of the theory, experience, if you have that experience, of rebirth.
He goes on to say what can be challenging about this for us.
I mean, it already sounds challenging.
Gil explains that how it's expressed makes it even harder for us to grok or embrace.
Gil writes:
*In line with the strong emphasis on purification, most of the descriptions of the ultimate goal are worded in the negative, describing what the liberated person has become freed from.

An enlightened person is free of death, free of bonds, free of conceit, free of the potential for rebirth, free of craving, fear, free of obsessive thinking, free of mental toxins and suffering and mental defilements of all kinds.
The more positive descriptions of the enlightened person are also seen as descriptions of absence.
Such a person is someone who has gone to the unconstructed immovable state, sometimes associated with the word nirvana, an ancient Indian language word suggesting extinguishing or release.*
Listing what you're freed from.
And there's rebirth again.
I've always been struck by this, too.
Especially in the early Buddhist teachings, there's always not this, not this, not this, not this.
No more of that, no more of that.
But what is it?
Our acquisitive minds want to know.
What do we get?
What's left when everything else is peeled away?
So Gil comments on that aspect of this, too.
He says:
*I can imagine a number of reasons why positive descriptions were avoided.
First, nirvana may be indescribable in terms of our experience and our language.
Second, the experience of the ultimate might not be one thing.
Rather, it may be like the condition of prisoners released from prison.
Each ex-prisoner shares the same freedom, freedom from incarceration, but each prisoner may vary widely in how they live with that freedom.
They may each have a very different experience of freedom.*
And freedom, actually, is one of the words that's used early on.
So freedom is a positive way to look at this.
Free.
Then the question is, free from what?
Well, I could list off a suggestion of what binds us.
Maybe some effect of deep, subtle desires, fears, hatreds, that's the usual trio of roots, right?
Root afflictions.
Greed, desire, fear, hatred, anger.
But maybe the core part of this practice, in both the first goal and the second goal, is for each of us to look and see.
If I were to be free from something, what would I be free of?
Do I know what binds me?
Or am I so used to the gilded cage that I don't notice?
What binds me?
What limits me?
Am I blind to ways I'm bound?
So this is an important question, I think.
What binds you?
What limits you?
And is it possible you become pretty habituated to that, so it really takes some time and some patience and practice to even notice?
Oh, wow.
Look at that.
I'm limited by that fear or that assumption or that prejudice or that belief or that situation, deeper away than I thought I was.
Look at how I'm avoiding that.
Wow.
And then each of us is probably different, even if we have this human heritage in common.
And so maybe Buddhism has two different goals: increased happiness, reduced suffering, and total and complete freedom.
If one may sound lesser, I wonder if that's really the intention, if one is lesser than the other.
But how do we approach this?
Well, it seems like there are two methods, too.
Two goals and two methods.
Maybe one we might call systematic methods: stuff to do, practices to take on, things to explore.
But maybe the second category might be something like trust methods.
Those are subtle, right, because you could also say non-methods, or you could just say trust.
You could just say trust.
So let's explore this possibility here.
Two goals and two methods.
Then we get a little grid.
I can apply the different methods to the different goals.
Systematic methods is what I was just talking about: inquiring, wondering.
What binds me?
What limits me?
What's my suffering?
What are its qualities?
And how can I meet them and break those bonds and heal from those layers of illness?
Maybe good to talk more to teachers or to take on a different practice or to listen to a trusted friend.
Do some trainings.
Find a good therapist.
Work with a therapist anywhere in the world right now.
Go to a teaching anywhere in the world, too.
And maybe there are steps and stages, and different systems have different steps and stages.
I just bought a big fat book by a guy named Kuladasa.
It was a ten-stage integrated Buddhist and Beyond Buddhist meditation program.
It was recommended to me.
I hope I can set aside some of my resistance and explore him fully.
So, systematic methods.
Then we have these trust methods.
Just practice.
What binds you is not a list of things to solve in the trust method, but maybe more like a knot in your heart.
And that resting in practice, you don't want to pick at the knot, it just makes it worse, right, to pick at the knot.
So in this model, maybe resting in practice with full attention and commitment, but deeply resting in practice, is like resting that knot in your heart in a warm bath.
Gradually it will soften, loosen up, and unravel.
And your life opens up.
So are these two methods for waking up, awakening, in conflict with each other?
In one frame, they could be a little suspicious of each other, I've noticed.
The systematic methods can be suspicious of the trust methods: "What are you people doing, just sitting there?
You don't know that much about your mind, you don't know that much about the teachings.
You're just lazy.
What's your deal?
You're not doing anything about this.
It's a very smart way: 30 plus years of sitting will get you what?"
So the systematic methods might be suspicious of the trust methods.
But the trust methods could also be suspicious, even though they're about trust.
Kind of ironic.
Trust methods could be suspicious of the systematic methods: "You're just running that hamster wheel there.
Every problem you find and solve, you're going to find another one, right?
Because you're in this modality of finding problems and trying to solve them.
You tie new bonds through all this striving, all this trying, all this effort.
Ah, God, exhausting just looking at you.
We're over here sitting peacefully in our trust [unclear: "sendo"]."
Another way to look at it is: what's the model behind it?
Are the systematic methods towards awakening saying you are broken?
"Sorry, but you are, yeah.
But lucky, good news, the powerful practices of Buddhism can heal you, make you whole again, solve all these problems, ultimately solve the whole problem of living and dying."
Wow.
And in that framework, the Buddha is often called the great physician, or the first physician, or the first psychologist later on when they had that word.
So maybe the systematic methods exist against a backdrop of brokenness.
Just feeling into these methods and ideas, not just in your head but in your gut.
And the trust methods could be saying something a little bit different.
Maybe the trust methods are saying, "You're already whole.
You're already healed.
It's okay.
What a shame that you have this powerful belief in your own brokenness.
Conditioned belief, right?
It's not your fault.

But good news: just practicing, relaxing into the practice, being so patient, eventually you'll, depending on who's talking, either remember your wholeness or, maybe even better, forget your brokenness, forget it so completely that you're just whole."
Feeling your wholeness.
It's really interesting contemplating all this.
It's full of philosophical stuff, even though it's very real, it's actual lived practice and life in our hearts.
And we practice all this against the background of the world, right?
I keep trying to reflect and understand that I've had a fairly privileged, maybe very privileged and protected life myself, born into a reasonably caring and functional family.
I had a few major upheavals, but basically that's true, supported within a middle class and rising status, with the opportunity of education and a minimum of unfair prejudice tripping me up.
It was like an interesting lark, like one of the few times I noticed that I was being discriminated against, I was like, "Wow, it's kind of interesting."
It wasn't so oppressive for me, right?
It's mostly interesting.
What a privilege to feel that way about prejudice.
And yet I've had plenty of struggles and suffering and confusion and tangledness.
Like we all do.

And I think I've practiced these two different methods and flowed back and forth between these two different models of brokenness and wholeness, and been interested in these two different goals: to be a little happier for sure, but also, what is this possibility of freedom?

The practice has helped me see more clearly what I've hidden from myself, helped me trust more, feel into my own goodness and the goodness of everybody around me, without exception, and to feel more and more trusted even when things do look bad.
They do look bad, right?
In so many ways.
There's a trusting that it is just how it seems to need to be, even when there's suffering, a lot of suffering.
And I've tried to get better at not turning away, not hanging out in my bubble too much.
Even when there's a Camp 220 in downtown Bellingham, with 100 of our neighbors shivering through the night in a storm.

And even when there are people in the mayor's office and the police department who have very good reasons to clear out Camp 220 and to break their agreement with the campers, even clear it out a day early, and start cleaning up the physical mess left behind, even as they in some way suffer, knowing they can't clean up the true mess.
That situation showed us yet again the inequitableness of our society.

But somehow the practice gives me trust, nonetheless, and I hope helps me take action: going down there to make a material donation, giving a little bigger donation to the food bank than I usually would have, which is a drop in the bucket, right?
But it's a real drop.
And a board member from the food bank called me and said, "Sweet, say thank you."
I'm like, "Wow, thank you, thank you, geez."
There's so much suffering, right?
But there are also so many bodhisattvas trying to alleviate that suffering.
All sides, whenever we think there are sides, so many bodhisattvas running around.

When Rizla and I dropped off our donation of old meditation cushions for padding, there were people running around trying to take care of the situation, even if the wind was blowing, the rain was coming down, it was so cold.
Bodhisattvas everywhere.
Now, we've talked before about the Buddhist model of the six realms, and how here in this human realm, the teachings keep suggesting that we have the suffering that we need.
Of course, there are a lot of things that could go sideways here from a social justice perspective, like, what?
So people of color get more from the human realm?
But this is the model, that the suffering is here to help us practice, help us learn, help us grow up as individuals, as society.
But they also say that it's a really, really slow ass project, right?
We chanted about millions, hundreds of millions of kalpas, is how long it takes to understand this.
And a kalpa, one kalpa, is a really, really long time, longer than we can imagine.

So, watching myself as best I can over 33 or 34 years of Zen practice, and having the good fortune to watch and listen to others in our sangha as we've all grown and changed together and suffered and learned and found more joy and peace and been spun out by anger and mistrust over the years, I think about planets orbiting each other.
Sometimes there's a close pass and either it feels really great or the planets grind into each other a little bit.
But little by little there's healing, for sure, no question.
And so much more is needed, for sure, no question.
And the main school we've received, of those two methods, is the trust method, deeply the trust method.
So I went back to Suzuki Roshi a bit, too, this morning.
I opened up Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind.
You can never open up Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind too many times.
Such a powerful expression of the trust method.
And throughout that he's really recommending don't get in this framework of enlightened and unenlightened.
I wonder if somewhere he's going tsk tsk tsk about this talk: "Tim, come on."
So here are a few quotations from Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind.
This is towards the end of the book, in the part called Beyond Consciousness.
First he gives us a framework for how we should hold our hearts in practice, the framework he suggests.
*We should establish our practice where there is no practice or enlightenment.
As long as we practice zazen in the area where there is practice and enlightenment, there's no chance to make perfect peace for ourselves.
We must firmly believe in our true nature.
Our true nature is beyond conscious experience.
It is only in our conscious experience that we find practice and enlightenment, good or bad.
But whether we have or don't have the experience of our true nature, what exists there, beyond consciousness, actually exists.
And it is there that we have to establish the foundation of our practice.
The foundation of our practice is beyond our consciousness, beyond our thinking.*
Suzuki Roshi has a different idea than Descartes.
How do we find that, I guess, right?
Wow.
He doesn't exactly give a systematic blueprint for how to get there, right?
Because this is the trust method, not so much the systematic method.
And yet this method has inspired hundreds, thousands, right?
For thousands of years.
And here we are today.
Even though in all these talks we rarely say anything that useful, really.
Someone says zazen is useless.
I don't know if he said that last week.
And that's what's great about it, because it's about the trust method.
One more Suzuki Roshi quote.
A little later in that section he says:
*Have a firm conviction in the original emptiness of your mind is the most important thing in your practice.
A firm conviction in the original emptiness of your mind is the most important thing in practice.
In Buddhist scriptures we sometimes use vast analogies in an attempt to describe empty mind.
We use astronomically great numbers.
So great it's beyond counting.
This means to give up calculating.
If it is so great that you cannot count it, you will lose your interest and eventually give up.
This kind of description may also give rise to a kind of interest in that enumerable number, which will help you stop the thinking of your small mind.*
There are two things here.
This is a trip, actually.
One paragraph of Suzuki Roshi.
It's a trip.
So the first part is just this firm conviction.
Trust.
The original emptiness of your mind.
Your mind beyond thinking.
But then he gives us this interesting study point.
So we shouldn't just go sitting around saying trust, trust, trust, trust.
He says we should study the teachings.
Why?
Because it's going to frustrate us.
That's why.
So this is like a really elaborate recommendation of Chris's Monday Night Dogen Group.
Getting into these far out teachings that seem beyond what you can understand will appropriately frustrate you, but at the same time you'll get interested.
He says you'll lose your interest and give up.
And by give up he doesn't mean give up practicing.
It means giving up thinking that you can understand it in that conscious mind way.
And the huge numbers thing is great too.
Try to figure out the innumerable number.
It'll keep your mind busy.
Stop thinking, or frustrate or overload the thinking of your small mind.
It's great.
And who knows what's truly possible through practice.
We can't know that.
So I want to close with another kind of long quotation and a little recording.
So I hope you're able to follow okay.
Good thing there's a recording.
I know when speakers give long quotations I often fall asleep.
So if you're asleep right now you're not hearing this, so it doesn't matter.
But this is a quotation from Chögyam Trungpa, from his early book Born in Tibet.
And Chris asked me for a title for the talk, and I had just read this quotation.
So I said something about lightness of being, or light.
So here's a story from Tibet that several reliable sources say happened.
So who are we to know?
There's Trungpa.
*At a place called [unclear: "Manikengo"] we had been told a story of a very saintly man who died there the previous year.
We went to the house where he had lived.
We met his son and his wife.
We had the miracle of what had occurred at the old man's death.
In his lifetime this man had erected a group of Mani stones on which he'd carved a great number of mantras and sutras.
He'd also set up a stupa among them.
In his youth this man had been a servant for a wealthy family, but in middle age he left employment to receive meditation instruction in the monastery.
Though he still had to work for his living by day, he spent most of his nights in contemplation, only allowing himself two or three hours sleep.
His compassion was so great that he always helped everyone in need and opened his house at all times to pilgrims and the very poor.
And while carrying out his daily work he used to practice meditation his own way.
Though his son, who was a monk, told him he should do the more formal spiritual practices, but this he didn't accept.*
*Then something strange happened.
Though he had hitherto been in good health, three years before his death he suddenly fell ill.
No explanation.
His family began to be very worried, yet he himself appeared to be increasingly happy.
He composed and sang his own songs of praise instead of traditional Buddhist chants.
As his illness became more and more serious, lamas and doctors were called in, with his son telling him he must now remember all the teachings he'd received.
At which point he smiled, saying, "I've forgotten it all, and anyway there's nothing to remember.
Everything is an illusion, yet I am confident and all is well."
Just before his death the old man said, "When I die you must not move my body for a week.
That is all I desire."*
*So he died, and they wrapped his dead body in old clothes and called in lamas and monks to recite and chant.
The body was carried into a small room a little bigger than the cupboard, and it was noted that although the old man had been quite tall, the body appeared to become a bit smaller.
At the same time a rainbow was seen over the house.
And on the sixth day, on looking into the room, the old man saw the body had grown still smaller.
The funeral service was arranged for the morning of the eighth day.
So the men came to take the body for the cremation, they undid the coverings, there was nothing inside except nails and hair.
The villagers were astonished, for it would have been impossible for anyone to come into the room.
The door was locked, the window was too small.
So nobody could have taken the body.*
And then it goes on.
I'll skip the next part, but the lamas were called and lamas confirmed that this could happen.
This is the practice of the rainbow body, practiced deeply, and after death your body dissolves into light, [unclear: "as pierces a rainbow"] over your house.
Apparently there are many reported instances of this, reliable reporters.
So what do we know?
Note in there again we have this interesting tension between systematic methods and trust methods.
And a powerful lay practitioner, like we are.
I do allow myself more than two or three hours of sleep, but we're all trying to practice every day and live our lives.
In this case the son goes to the monastery and gets the systematic stuff, and the father just figures out his own way of practice with great trust.
He's ready to die, the son says, "Remember the teachings," and he says, "Oh, no problem, I forgot them all."
Perfect.
And then later on, actually, Trungpa describes the son actually kind of left the monastery after that.
He's like, whoa.
His world got turned upside down.
His father could have this incredible spiritual experience or feat or something without being a monk.
So I don't know what you make of such stories of miracles.
Maybe you thought miracles only happened in other practices.
